title: A window start aligned by a mask on power-of-two windows and by the remainder elsewhere proved equal
summary: The same rewrite of Crosscut's `Window` counter done right: a window that is a power of two aligns its start by clearing the reading's low bits, `nowNanos & -windowNanos`, the fast path for the filter's default windows, and any other window by the remainder as before. The regression proof shows the counter unchanged on every counter, reading and window: the tool's own checker in 0.5 s, the division left to the solver under the facts of every division, among them that a power of two divides by masking; JBMC did not finish the same harness within a minute.

change.description: Compute the window's start as `nowNanos & -windowNanos` when `windowNanos` is a power of two (`(windowNanos & (windowNanos - 1)) == 0`) and as `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos` otherwise. The tests are unchanged.

risk: None: the proof is over every counter, clock reading and window length, the same result record or the same exception in both versions. What is at stake is the review of a bit trick: that `nowNanos & -windowNanos` is the alignment exactly on the windows the condition selects, which the proof settles without the reviewer working through two's complement.
explanation: The harness builds the counter from symbolic components, calls both versions on the same reading and window, and compares the result records component by component, or the exceptions by class. On a window that is a power of two, `-windowNanos` is the complement of `windowNanos - 1`, so the mask clears exactly the bits the remainder removes from a non-negative reading (readings are non-negative: a counter's start is, and a reading before it throws); on any other window the two versions run the same remainder, the same bits in the checker. The tool's own checker proves it in 0.5 s over 10 paths and 17 solver calls, with the one division built in full after a probe's model got it wrong; JBMC did not finish within 60 s.
resolution: Merge. The condition is the claim the comment in example 136 made, now checked by the code rather than assumed, and the proof is the review of the trick.
notes: No scope: the proof covers every input, including windows that are not powers of two, where both versions take the remainder, and the inputs both versions refuse (a non-positive window, a reading before the start, a count that overflows into the constructor's check), where both throw `IllegalArgumentException`.

The tool's own checker leaves `nowNanos % windowNanos` to the solver as bits under what holds of every division: the remainder is smaller than the divisor and takes the dividend's sign, a division by one is exact, and a power of two divides a non-negative dividend with the remainder `dividend & (divisor - 1)`. On the masking path that last fact is what relates the old start to the new; on the other path both versions use the same remainder bits. The circuit of the division is built only when the solver's model of a branch side gets the remainder wrong, once here, and the log (`bmc.log` in the work directory) says `1 of 1 divisions and 0 of 0 multiplications built in full`. Before the facts, the checker took 12 s on 135's one remainder and did not finish 134's scoped harness in two minutes.

The other side of a branch is asked of the solver only for as long as its calls so far took together, at least a second; a side it has not refuted by then is explored once the decided paths are done, with the time left. A proof with an infeasible side that is hard to refute (that a value is not a multiple of another) loses at most the probe's time; a violation on the feasible side is found without waiting, which is how JBMC's one formula finds 134's.

JBMC, with its default solver, did not finish the same harness within 60 s, nor 135's with its own arithmetic refinement (`--refine-arithmetic`); the mask and the remainder in one formula over 64-bit values are what it struggles with, where the checker's facts settle the mask side without the divider. A rewrite to `nowNanos / windowNanos * windowNanos`, the divide-and-multiply form of the same alignment, neither engine proved within a minute when this example was written: it rests on the identity of a 64-bit division and multiplication, which the facts do not include. Since then the checker rewrites a quotient times its divisor as the dividend less the remainder, the identity itself, and proves that form in 0.1 s: example 138.
provenance: Constructed as the correct form of example 136's rewrite, on the same kernel of Crosscut, to show the tool's own checker proving a power-of-two mask equal to a remainder on every input with the division left to the solver.
